First convert the given emission energy to a wavelength so we know what color is emitted.

E (eV) = 1240 eV·nm / λ (nm)  ⇒ λ = 1240 / 2.3393 ≈ 531 nm

A wavelength of ~530 nm is in the green region of the visible spectrum, so the dye fluoresces green light.

In fluorescence, the photon that is absorbed always has a higher energy (shorter wavelength) than the photon that is emitted, because some energy is lost non-radiatively before emission (Stokes shift). Therefore the light absorbed must be at a shorter wavelength (higher energy) than green—i.e. in the blue/violet part of the spectrum.

Comparing the options:
• Yellow and red are longer-wavelength (lower-energy) than green, so they cannot be the absorbed light.  
• Violet is higher in energy than blue, but typical organic dyes that emit near 530 nm usually absorb in the blue (~470–500 nm), not as far into the violet (~400 nm).  
• Blue light (≈ 460–490 nm, ≈ 2.5–2.7 eV) is just the right energy range to be slightly higher than the 2.34 eV emission.

Hence the dye most plausibly absorbs blue light.

Answer: D
